misconception_description: Student believes that values must be explicitly converted to their current type to ensure type safety.

solutions.generated_code:
program BilanganTerbesarDariDigit
kamus
  d1, d2, d3, d4, temp : integer
algoritma
  input(d1, d2, d3, d4)
  d1 <- integer(d1)
  d2 <- integer(d2)
  d3 <- integer(d3)
  d4 <- integer(d4)
  if integer(d1) < integer(d2) then
    temp <- integer(d1)
    d1 <- integer(d2)
    d2 <- integer(temp)
  endif
  if integer(d2) < integer(d3) then
    temp <- integer(d2)
    d2 <- integer(d3)
    d3 <- integer(temp)
  endif
  if integer(d3) < integer(d4) then
    temp <- integer(d3)
    d3 <- integer(d4)
    d4 <- integer(temp)
  endif
  if integer(d1) < integer(d2) then
    temp <- integer(d1)
    d1 <- integer(d2)
    d2 <- integer(temp)
  endif
  if integer(d2) < integer(d3) then
    temp <- integer(d2)
    d2 <- integer(d3)
    d3 <- integer(temp)
  endif
  if integer(d1) < integer(d2) then
    temp <- integer(d1)
    d1 <- integer(d2)
    d2 <- integer(temp)
  endif
  output(integer(d1) * 1000 + integer(d2) * 100 + integer(d3) * 10 + integer(d4))
endprogram

metadata.modification_notes: The student adds explicit int() conversions throughout the code even though the values are already integers. They convert len(arr) to int even though len() returns an int, convert arr[0] and arr[i] to int even though array elements are already ints, convert n to int in the range, convert num to int before operations, and even convert the literal 10 and final return value to int. The student genuinely believes these conversions are necessary for type safety and proper functioning. The code still works correctly since converting an integer to an integer is a no-op, just with unnecessary overhead.
